title: Esther 5:9–14
context: Haman leaves the banquet joyful, but when Mordecai at the king’s gate neither rises nor moves for him, he is filled with wrath (5:9). He restrains himself, goes home, gathers his friends and Zeresh his wife, and boasts of his wealth, his many children, his promotion, and his private invitation to the queen’s banquets, yet says that all of it avails him nothing while he sees Mordecai the Jew at the king’s gate (5:10–13). Zeresh and his friends advise him to have a gallows fifty cubits high made and to ask the king in the morning to hang Mordecai on it, and the idea pleases Haman (5:14). The structure is often called a gallows; the Hebrew word is commonly understood to mean a wooden pole or stake, and readers differ on whether hanging, impaling, or exposure is in view. The stated height is unusually great, and many readers take it as meant to make the execution very public, while others see exaggeration; this commentary does not fix the details. The scene sets up the reversal in which Haman himself is hanged on it (7:9–10). The book does not name God here, and the passage is handled soberly as a plan for an unjust killing.

verses.text: Then Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart, but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, that he didn’t stand up nor move for him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman leaves joyful, but the sight of Mordecai refusing to stand or move for him fills him with wrath. Arminian readers see how fragile pride-driven joy is, since a single slight can overturn it, and they note that Mordecai’s continued refusal is a consistent, chosen stance even after the decree has been issued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the sudden swing from joy to rage as exposing a heart ruled by self-regard, and they see Mordecai’s steadiness as quiet faithfulness under threat. Shared ground: both traditions read Haman’s volatility as a moral portrait, note that the text again does not state Mordecai’s reasons beyond what 3:4 reported, and avoid inventing them.

verses.text: Nevertheless Haman restrained himself, and went home. There, he sent and called for his friends and Zeresh his wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman restrains himself, goes home, and calls his friends and his wife Zeresh. Arminian readers note that he can control outward behavior while his inner anger grows, a picture of the difference between self-restraint and true change of heart. He seeks counsel that will feed rather than check his rage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the restraint as outward only and see the gathering of friends as seeking affirmation rather than wisdom. They note that Zeresh and the friends will reappear when Haman’s fortunes turn (6:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as moving Haman toward a fateful plan and see the choice of counselors as revealing his character.

verses.text: Haman recounted to them the glory of his riches, the multitude of his children, all the things in which the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman boasts of his wealth, his many children, and his promotion above the princes and servants. Arminian readers see the emptiness of a life measured by status and possessions, and they note the irony of a man counting blessings that will soon be lost. The boast shows how freely he has given himself to pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the boast as a portrait of pride before a fall (compare Proverbs 16:18) and note that his ten sons are later named in 9:7–10. They see God’s sovereignty over the rise and fall of the proud. Shared ground: both traditions read Haman’s boasting as moral warning and see it as setting up the reversal that follows.

verses.text: Haman also said, “Yes, Esther the queen let no man come in with the king to the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and tomorrow I am also invited by her together with the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman adds that the queen invited only him with the king, and that he is invited again tomorrow. Arminian readers note the dramatic irony, since Haman thinks the invitation honors him when it actually leads to his exposure. His misreading shows how pride blinds a person to reality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the irony and see providence in the hidden direction of events, with Haman confident in the very setting that will undo him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heightening the irony of the story, and both note that Haman does not know Esther’s identity, which remains hidden from him until 7:3–6.

verses.text: Yet all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”
verses.arminianNotes: Haman says that all his honors avail him nothing while he sees Mordecai the Jew at the king’s gate. Arminian readers see how a grudge can poison every good gift, and they stress that Haman chooses to let resentment rule him. The label “Mordecai the Jew” shows that his hatred is aimed at a people as well as a person.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as exposing the restless discontent of a proud heart, which no amount of honor can satisfy. They see in it a warning about covetous and resentful desire. Shared ground: both traditions read Haman’s words as a revealing confession, and both note that his fixation on Mordecai drives the plot toward the reversal in chapters 6–7.

verses.text: Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, “Let a gallows be made fifty cubits high, and in the morning speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on it. Then go in merrily with the king to the banquet.” This pleased Haman, so he had the gallows made.
verses.arminianNotes: Zeresh and the friends propose a gallows fifty cubits high and a morning request to hang Mordecai, and the idea pleases Haman. Arminian readers treat the plan soberly as a scheme for an unjust killing, freely chosen by Haman and encouraged by those around him. They hold that God never wills such murder, though he can bring good from the reversal that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the plan as wicked and note the irony that Haman will be hanged on the very structure he prepared (7:9–10; compare Psalm 7:15–16). They hold that God governs these events without approving the evil. Shared ground: both traditions handle the gallows soberly, leave the exact form and height open, and see the reversal as part of God’s justice.
